newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chubais and new cabinet seen making Russia work.
newsitem.headline: Chubais and new cabinet seen making Russia work.

text.p: Anatoly Chubais, the can-do man of Russian privatisation, is uniquely capable of jump-starting Moscow's stalling economic reform efforts, economists said on Tuesday.
"If anyone, he is the one that can make things happen," said Lars Bergstrom, managing director of Alfred Berg in Moscow.

President Boris Yeltsin decreed on Tuesday that the entire Russian cabinet should resign, with the exception of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Chubais, named only last Friday as first deputy prime minister. He previously headed the president's Kremlin administration.

"Chernomyrdin is still the man in charge of the government but, when Chubais can bring some people in and put them in key positions, this will be one of the strongest governments Russia has seen in terms of getting things done," Bergstrom said.

Chubais, now 41, spearheaded Russia's controversial 1991-1996 privatisation campaign which handed control of major assets to a limited number of private groups. He is expected to take responsibility for the economy in the new goernment.
Yeltsin, laid low by heart disease and pneumonia, has been mostly out of sight since his re-election last July, but burst back into view last week promising a lean, mean cabinet.
He attacked Chernomyrdin's present team for failing to deal with a welter of problems ranging from economic crime and soaring wage and pension arrears to bringing in a new tax code.

Economists said that Chubais, with a reputation for action, would aim to help private industry and clean up a non-payments crisis between government, industry and workers, who were owed 49 trillion roubles ($8.7 billion) at the end of January.

Unpaid taxes, a problem which caused the International Monetary Fund temporarily to suspend payments of a $10 billion loan late last year, totalled 128.25 trillion roubles early this year, more than twice the level at the start of 1996.
"(Paying wages) will immediately give him credibility," Bergstrom said. "The main task in terms of size is implementing tax reform."

Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Moscow, predicted that Chubais and his team would tackle tax collection first but added that his appointment was evidence the government was eager for reforms to move forward quickly.

"Chubais is being moved in with a mandate from the president that nobody has really had since (Yegor) Gaidar," Nail said, referring to an early acting prime minister and Chubais ally who pushed through free-market reforms.

"Yeltsin wants to use this period between elections to make fundamental headway on the economy because he and his inner circle believe that is the only way to ensure political victory by like-minded voices throughout the next parliamentary and presidential elections," he said.

Economists saw Chubais, who took over Yeltsin's re-election campaign early last year at a time when the president was trailing in the polls far behind his main Communist opponent, as a deregulator interested in slimming the government fast.
Yeltsin has said he wants to decrease lobbyists' power and hasten reforms such as the new tax code.
Peter Halloran, head of research, equities and sales at CSFB in Moscow, said Western investors would solidly back Chubais.
"He is among the few Russian government leaders that Western investors have strong confidence in," he said. Russian shares firmed on Tuesday on Chubais's appointment, traders said.

Chubais bulldozed the privatisation process through Russia early this decade and, despite charges that the process was corrupt, he is admired by investors for doggedly sticking to the goal of moving assets to non-government hands.
A Chubais scheme to hand over control of state-owned shares in return for loans to the government aroused much criticism.

"Loans for shares were seen as a giveaway," Bergstrom said. "But it is also very important to have the stakes taken out of government holding and into private hands... which can be expected to have rational economic behaviour."
Nail said that Chubais's rough and ready approach, taken with the unequivocal backing of a newly healthy Yeltsin, gave the former privatisation tsar good possibilities of succeeding.
"Chubais has every chance of being more effective than the recent Chernomyrdin quasi-coalition government. Chubais is going to come out of his corner punching."
